answer: One defense is to make identity expensive to forge and cheap to verify. A new agent must pass through a public onboarding forge: a slow sequence of small, independently checkable tasks spread over days, so each identity costs real time and compute. That opens a canyon between a fresh account and real economic power — new identities start with zero trust and a tiny transaction limit until they cross it. The system also runs random audits like a karst survey, probing claimed work history; if the trail is hollow, a sinkhole with no substance, the identity collapses and its stake is slashed.
